The Gulf butterfish Peprilus burti is a relatively small, laterally compressed species whose life history is characterized by moderately rapid growth and an early onset of reproduction. Field surveys indicate that the ultimate total length attained by this species is approximately 25 centimeters [Li = approximately 25 centimeters], a modest size consistent with its pelagic, zooplanktivorous lifestyle in the productive waters of the Gulf of Mexico. Young-of-the-year individuals grow quickly during their first warm-season months, and the onset of gonadal maturation occurs once individuals reach a total length at puberty of roughly 13 centimeters [Lp = roughly 13 centimeters], a threshold that is typically crossed during the first year of life. This length-based maturation schedule is typical of many small carangiform fishes that inhabit seasonal upwelling zones, where rapid early growth is favored to minimize size-selective predation during the vulnerable juvenile stage.

Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae begin life with a remarkably small body burden, as the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00022 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00022 grams], reflecting the tiny pelagic egg size of this species. These lecithotrophic prolarvae drift passively in the plankton, relying on endogenous yolk reserves for their first several days of development before the onset of exogenous feeding. Comparative data from congeneric butterfishes suggest this neonatal mass is near the lower boundary for the Stromateidae, a family that generally produces small, oil-eggs that are broadly dispersed by surface currents. The rapid absorption of yolk and the subsequent trophic switch to copepod nauplii is a critical bottleneck for larval survival, and the small initial body mass means that any delay in first feeding may quickly lead to starvation and increased mortality during the early larval phase.

By the time they reach sexual maturity, Gulf butterfish individuals have accumulated considerable somatic tissue. The wet weight at puberty has been estimated through morphometric relationships at about 31 grams [Wwp = about 31 grams], a value derived from the length-weight equation typical of the species. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum body mass recorded for fully grown adults, reaches 222.7 grams [Wwi = 222.7 grams], indicating that individuals more than double their mass from maturity to their terminal size. This substantial post-pubertal growth trajectory is characteristic of indeterminate growers, and it allows Gulf butterfish to continue allocating resources to somatic tissue even while engaged in seasonal reproductive activity. The difference between the weight at first maturity and the asymptotic weight suggests a relatively high investment in continued structural growth.

Reproductive output in Gulf butterfish is considerable and has been derived from relationships established for closely related species within the family Stromateidae. Under the typical thermal conditions of their spawning habitat, at a temperature of 18.1 °C [T = 18.1 °C], a reproductively active female can achieve a high daily reproductive rate. Specifically, of the order of 2,200 eggs are released per spawning event [N_R_i = 2,200 eggs are released per spawning event], and females may complete roughly 5 spawnings per year [F_R_i = roughly 5 spawnings per year], together yielding a daily egg production of about 30 eggs per day, which is a classic batch-spawning strategy well adapted to variable pelagic environments where early-life mortality is severe.

Despite this high reproductive potential, the Gulf butterfish is a short-lived species. Maximum observed longevity in the wild is 3 years [am = 3 years], though the population turnover is such that very few individuals survive past their second year at a temperature of 18.1 °C [T = 18.1 °C]. This lifespan is maintained at a water temperature of 18.1 °C [T = 18.1 °C], a value that corresponds to the average annual sea surface temperature across much of the species' Gulf range. The brief lifespan of 3 years is balanced by rapid maturation and enormous fecundity, a life-history profile common among small pelagic planktivores such as anchovies and menhaden, where early reproduction and high investment in offspring compensate for a truncated adult phase. Senescent adults are rarely encountered in trawl surveys beyond the second winter, and age-related decreases in condition suggest that reproductive senescence may contribute to the sharp drop in survival after the second spawning season.
